method: Built from the nine sweep files and three verify files in this folder. An item holds every sweep record that the verifiers held, or that stands single-source at medium or high confidence; refuted records and single-source low records are left out (listed under excluded). Records naming the same wine, dish or drink are merged; several vintages or formats of one wine are one item with each price labelled. Descriptions use the sourced facts plus general knowledge of the grape, place, producer, dish or drink; house facts are marked as what the list or menu prints. pairs_with names suggested partners from this catalogue and the pack; they are pairing advice, not house facts. Search snippets only: no page was read.

items.description: Krug, founded in Reims in 1843 by Joseph Krug, is one of the most celebrated Champagne houses, and its Grande Cuvée is the prestige blend at the heart of the house. The house drinks page prints Krug 'Grand Cuvée' Brut NV under Champagne Half Bottles at $305.00 (Krug itself spells it Grande Cuvée). Grande Cuvée blends Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier from many villages and well over a hundred wines across more than ten vintages, including old reserve wines, so each release, labeled by its Édition number, is a composition rather than a single year. The base wines ferment in small oak casks, and the wine ages on its lees for about seven years before release. Expect a rich, toasty, layered Champagne: brioche, hazelnut, candied citrus, honey and a fine, persistent bead with great freshness. It ages gracefully for a decade or more. A half bottle is perfect for two glasses of something special. It is superb with Grand Isle oysters, crab claws or Eggs Hussarde.

items.description: Billecart-Salmon is a family-run Champagne house in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, founded in 1818 and still known for elegance and finesse. The house drinks page prints Billecart-Salmon 'Brennan's 80th Anniversary' Brut Sous Bois Champagne FR NV (Oak Aged) as a 1.5L magnum at $350.00, under Champagne Large Format. Brennan's opened in 1946, so 2026 is its 80th year, and the label is a special bottling for the anniversary. Sous Bois means under wood: Billecart's Sous Bois cuvée is fermented and aged entirely in oak barrels, from roughly equal parts Meunier, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, according to third-party retail pages the sweep noted. The oak gives a rounder, richer, more vinous Champagne with notes of baked apple, brioche, toasted nuts and spice, while the house style keeps it fresh and precise. Magnums age more slowly and gracefully than standard bottles. Present it as the house's own anniversary Champagne, a once-only bottle for celebrations. It suits richer dishes: Redfish Véronique, Pecan Gulf Fish or the Duck Confit Waffle.

items.description: Bollinger, founded in Aÿ in 1829, is one of the great family-owned Champagne houses, known for a powerful, Pinot Noir driven style. The house drinks page prints Bollinger "Special Cuvée" Brut NV as a 1.5 L magnum at $450.00 under Champagne Large Format, and a fresh search repeated that line. Special Cuvée is typically around 60 percent Pinot Noir with Chardonnay and Meunier, much of it from grand and premier cru villages. Part of the wine ferments in old oak barrels, and the house keeps reserve wines in magnums under cork, which adds depth and complexity. Expect a full, rich Champagne with ripe apple, pear, brioche, toasted walnuts and a long, firm finish. It has the weight to stand up to food, and the magnum format keeps it fresh and lively. Describe it as Champagne with body and confidence, a great choice for a table that wants one bottle through several courses. It shines with the crab claws, steak tartare cannoli and Roost Burger.

items.description: Taittinger is one of the few major Champagne houses still run by its founding family, based in Reims and known for a Chardonnay-led, elegant style. Expect a light, fresh, delicate Champagne: white peach, citrus, flowers, a hint of brioche and a fine, creamy bead. It is a crowd-pleaser, and the 3L double magnum makes a showpiece for a party. Recommend the bottle as the easy happy hour choice, and the double magnum for celebrations. It pairs with oysters, fried snacks, crab claws and Eggs Benedict.

items.description: Billecart-Salmon, founded in 1818 in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, is admired for finesse, low dosage and very cold, slow fermentations that preserve freshness. The house happy hour page prints Billecart-Salmon Brut Réserve Champagne NV as a 1.5L magnum, originally $220, offered at $140.00 during Bubbles at Brennan's. The Brut Réserve is the house's signature non-vintage blend, built from Meunier, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with a large share of reserve wine for depth. Expect an elegant, precise Champagne: crisp apple, pear, lemon zest, white flowers, a little toast and a silky, fine mousse. The magnum keeps the wine particularly fresh and makes it ideal for a group in the courtyard. Billecart also made the house's 80th Anniversary Sous Bois magnum, so this is a good way to introduce the producer at a friendlier price. Describe it as polished, fresh and graceful. It pairs well with oysters, the Creole Caesar, fried pickles and Eggs Sardou.

items.description: Charles Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1851 by Charles-Camille Heidsieck, the original Champagne Charlie, who famously sold Champagne in America in the 1800s. The house is now prized for its deep reserve wines and its chalk cellars, the crayères of Reims. The Bubbles at Brennan's page prints Charles Heidsieck Brut Rosé Réserve Champagne NV, originally $225, at $145 during happy hour. The rosé is made by blending a portion of red Pinot Noir wine into a base built from Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, with a generous share of reserve wines. It ages on the lees for several years. Expect a rich, complex rosé with red berries, cherry, blood orange, brioche, spice and a creamy texture. It has the weight to pair with food, not just aperitif snacks. Describe it as the most serious rosé on the Bubbles list. It is excellent with the duck confit waffle, shrimp and grits, the Roost Burger or Cherries Jubilee.

items.description: Pommery was made famous by Madame Louise Pommery, who took over the Reims house after her husband's death in 1858 and created one of the first dry Brut Champagnes in 1874, when most Champagne was sweet. The house cellars run through ancient Roman chalk pits under the city. A Tock listing prints a Sabering Class ticket at $120 plus tax, gratuity included, which lets one guest learn to saber a bottle of Pommery Brut Royal Champagne NV, with a $20 plus tax spectator ticket that includes one glass. The verifier notes the current listing is International Champagne Day, Friday 23 October 2026, with classes in the courtyard. Brut Royal blends Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier from many villages. Expect a light, fresh, crisp Champagne with citrus, white fruit, flowers and a delicate bead, built for elegance. Sabering means striking the neck of a chilled bottle with the back of a saber so the collar breaks cleanly away. It pairs with oysters, crab claws and fried snacks.

items.description: Domaine François Raveneau is, with Vincent Dauvissat, one of the two most revered names in Chablis, a small family estate now run by Bernard and Jean-Marie Raveneau. Its wines are made from Chardonnay, fermented and aged in old oak barrels and feuillettes, the small local casks, which give texture without any taste of new wood. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Raveneau "Butteaux" 1er Cru Chablis in 1.5L magnum, 2014 at $840 and 2015 at $800. Butteaux sits within the Montmains premier cru, on Kimmeridgian limestone full of fossil oyster shells, the soil that gives Chablis its flinty, saline character. Expect lemon, green apple, oyster shell, white flowers and smoky minerality, with power and a long finish. Raveneau's wines are famous for aging twenty years or more, and magnums age even more slowly, so these are just entering their prime. They belong on a Grand Award list as benchmark Chablis in a rare format. Pour with oysters, crab claws or Redfish Véronique.

items.description: Domaine Christian Moreau Père et Fils was created in 2002 when Christian Moreau and his son Fabien took back their family vineyards after the sale of the old Moreau négociant business. The estate's jewel is the Clos des Hospices, a small walled parcel within Les Clos, the largest and most celebrated of the seven Chablis grands crus. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Christian Moreau "Les Clos, Clos des Hospices" 2012 at $210; the format is assumed to be a bottle. Les Clos lies on a steep southwest-facing slope of Kimmeridgian limestone, producing Chablis of depth, structure and intense minerality. Moreau ferments partly in oak and partly in steel. Expect ripe citrus, pear, honey, flint and a saline, long finish; at fourteen years old, the 2012 should show added notes of hazelnut, beeswax and toast. Grand cru Chablis ages beautifully, and this is a mature bottle at a fair price. It is excellent with Pecan Gulf Fish, crab claws and Redfish Véronique.

items.description: Domaine Billaud-Simon is a historic Chablis estate founded in 1815, now owned by the Faiveley family and known for pure, precise wines made mostly in stainless steel. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Domaine Billaud-Simon "Blanchot" 2016 at $230; the format is assumed to be a bottle. Blanchot is the easternmost of the seven Chablis grands crus, facing southeast, which gives it a cooler exposure and a more delicate, floral, finely mineral style than its neighbors. Chablis is made from Chardonnay grown on Kimmeridgian limestone, which shows in the wine as a flinty, saline freshness. Expect white flowers, lemon, green apple, chalk and a long, elegant finish; at ten years, the 2016 adds hazelnut and honey. Grand cru Chablis from a careful producer ages well for fifteen years or more. Present it as an elegant, refined grand cru. It suits oysters, the Creole Caesar and Gulf Fish en Papillote.

items.description: Raveneau is one of the two legendary estates of Chablis, and its grand cru wines are among the most sought-after white wines in the world. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Domaine François Raveneau "Blanchot" 2018 at $1,255, and a fresh Binwise snippet repeated that line; the format is assumed to be a bottle. Raveneau owns a small holding in Blanchot, the easternmost grand cru, known for finesse and floral elegance. The estate hand-harvests Chardonnay, ferments with native yeasts and ages the wine in old barrels and feuillettes, so it gains texture without new oak flavors. Expect citrus, white peach, flowers, oyster shell, smoke and a long, saline, mineral finish. 2018 was a warm, ripe year, so the wine is generous but still tightly built. Raveneau's grands crus need years to open; this one will improve for another decade. It belongs on a Grand Award list as one of Burgundy's rarest whites. Pour it with oysters, crab claws or Redfish Véronique.

The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Domaine Jean Collet et Fils "Valmur" 2020 at $195; the format is assumed to be a bottle. items.description: Domaine Vincent Dauvissat, also labeled René et Vincent Dauvissat, is one of the two most celebrated estates in Chablis alongside Raveneau, and the two families are related. The estate farms organically and makes tiny quantities. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Domaine Vincent Dauvissat "Les Clos" 2023 at $440; the format is assumed to be a bottle. Les Clos is the largest and most powerful of the seven grands crus, on a steep, sunny slope of Kimmeridgian limestone. Dauvissat ferments and ages its wines in old barrels and feuillettes, producing Chablis of great depth and precision. Expect lemon, green apple, white flowers, crushed oyster shell and a powerful, saline finish that lingers. As a 2023, this wine is very young: it will taste tight and electric now and improve for fifteen years or more. Decanting helps. It belongs on a Grand Award list as one of the benchmark wines of Chablis. Pour with oysters, crab claws or Gulf fish.

items.description: Raveneau's Montée de Tonnerre is often called the finest premier cru in Chablis, a wine many collectors rank alongside grand cru. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Domaine François Raveneau "Montée de Tonnerre" 2020 at $1,035 and 2022 at $920; the format is assumed to be a bottle. Montée de Tonnerre lies just across a small valley from the grands crus, on the same Kimmeridgian limestone, facing southeast. Raveneau hand-harvests, ferments with native yeasts and ages the wine in old barrels and feuillettes for about a year and a half. items.description: Damien Martin is a young grower in Burgundy making small quantities of regional and village wines with a fresh, natural style. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Pinot Noir from Damien Martin, Burgundy, 2023, and the verifier confirms that the house guide carries it as the $17 glass. Bourgogne Rouge is the regional appellation for red Burgundy, made from Pinot Noir grown across the Côte d'Or and surrounding areas. The grapes are typically fermented in vats and aged in older barrels, so the wine shows fruit rather than oak. items.description: Romanée-Conti is the most famous vineyard in the world: a monopole of less than two hectares in Vosne-Romanée, owned entirely by the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti and producing only a few thousand bottles a year. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, holds Romanée-Conti Grand Cru across several vintages from 2007 to 2022, ranging from $12,500 to $16,000 depending on vintage. Individual vintages and their prices are not itemized in the snippet, so read each on the list. The vineyard has been prized since the Middle Ages and takes its name from the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760. The domaine farms biodynamically, harvests late and ferments with whole clusters. Expect an ethereal, layered Pinot Noir: red and black fruit, rose petal, exotic spice, forest floor and silky, endless length. It needs decades to reach its peak. A range of vintages is an extraordinary statement for a Grand Award cellar. Requests should go through the sommelier. It pairs with the Hazelnut-Crusted Duck or Roasted Chateaubriand.

The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Camille Giroud Chambertin Grand Cru 2006 at $540. Chambertin, in Gevrey-Chambertin, is one of the most famous grands crus of Burgundy and was said to be Napoleon's favorite wine. It produces powerful, structured Pinot Noir, deep in color and built to age. Expect black cherry, plum, game, earth, leather and spice, with firm tannins softened by time. At twenty years old, the 2006 should be fully mature, with savory, truffle and forest floor notes. 2006 was a sound, classic vintage. A mature grand cru at this price is a smart recommendation for guests who want Burgundy ready to drink. It pairs with the Hazelnut-Crusted Duck, Roasted Chateaubriand and the veal grillades.

items.description: Jean Foillard is one of the original Gang of Four, the Morgon growers who in the 1980s, inspired by the ideas of the scientist and négociant Jules Chauvet, revived natural, low-intervention Beaujolais and showed how serious Gamay can be. The Binwise list, as a search summary prints it, includes Jean Foillard "Côte du Py" Morgon in 1.5L magnum, 2023 at $250 and 2024 at $270, and a fresh Binwise snippet repeated both lines; the sweep notes the 2024 format is assumed to be magnum by its placement, so confirm. Côte du Py is an old volcanic hill in Morgon with decomposed blue schist soils, giving the most structured and age-worthy wines of the cru. Foillard uses whole-cluster, semi-carbonic fermentation with native yeasts and little sulfur. Expect dark cherry, raspberry, violet, pepper and a mineral, savory finish, juicy but with real depth. Côte du Py can age a decade or more, especially in magnum. Present it as cru Beaujolais at its finest, perfect for a group. It pairs with the gumbo, the Duck Confit Waffle and the burger.

Boal, also spelled Bual, is the medium-sweet style among the four noble grapes, richer than Sercial and Verdelho but less sweet than Malmsey. Vintage Madeira must spend at least twenty years in cask. Expect amber color, with notes of caramel, toffee, dried fig, raisin, walnut, coffee, orange peel and spice, balanced by Madeira's signature lively acidity. A 58 year old wine by the glass is rare. items.description: Bodegas El Maestro Sierra is a small, traditional Sherry house in Jerez, Spain, founded in 1830 and for decades run by Pilar Plá, one of the region's most respected figures, known for old, hand-tended soleras. The house dessert menu PDF, as a search summary prints it, lists El Maestro Sierra Pedro Ximénez Sherry at $11, presumed per glass. Pedro Ximénez, or PX, is both a grape and a style: the grapes are dried in the sun until they become raisins, then pressed, fortified and aged in a solera, the Sherry system of blending younger and older wines in stacked barrels. The result is the sweetest wine on the menu, almost black in color and syrupy in texture. Expect raisin, fig, date, molasses, coffee, chocolate and licorice. It is famously poured over vanilla ice cream in Spain. It pairs with the bread pudding, the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and Bananas Foster.

items.description: The Sazerac is the official cocktail of New Orleans and one of America's oldest mixed drinks, tied to the Sazerac Coffee House of the 1850s and to Antoine Peychaud, the apothecary whose bitters are its signature. The cocktails page prints Brennan's Classic Sazerac as Sazerac Rye Whiskey, Herbsaint rinse and Peychaud's bitters, at $13.00. The build is simple and exact: a chilled rocks glass is rinsed with Herbsaint, an anise liqueur made in New Orleans, and the excess discarded. In a mixing glass, rye, Peychaud's bitters and a little sugar are stirred with ice, then strained into the rinsed glass, neat, with no ice. A lemon peel is traditionally expressed over the top. The drink tastes of spicy rye, red-fruited, anise-scented bitters and a ghost of licorice from the rinse, strong and aromatic. Describe it as the city's drink, served the old way. It sits beside Thompson's Dream and Origin Story on the Sazerac list. With food, it suits rich dishes like the Roost Burger or turtle soup.

items.description: Chateaubriand is the thick center cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted whole and carved for two, a dish French kitchens named for the writer and statesman François-René de Chateaubriand. The menu prints it as Creekstone Farms beef tenderloin, serves two, at $120.00. Creekstone is a Kansas producer of Black Angus beef known for consistent marbling. The cut is seared hard, roasted to temperature and rested so the juices settle, then sliced at an angle into thick medallions. Tenderloin is the most tender muscle on the animal and mild in flavor, so the pleasure is the texture, buttery and yielding, with a browned, savory crust. items.description: Turtle soup is one of the defining dishes of Creole New Orleans: a dark, rich, roux-based soup with a long history in the city's grand old dining rooms. The menu prints Brennan's version as 100% turtle meat, brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged sherry, at $13.00. It also appears as a first course choice in the house Thanksgiving menu summary. The base is a brown roux cooked slowly with the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper, tomato and stock, then the turtle meat simmers until tender. Spinach and hard-cooked egg are the traditional garnishes, and sherry is the signature finish: many New Orleans dining rooms pour a little at the table so the guest can add more to taste. Expect a deep, savory, slightly tangy bowl with a warm, nutty lift from the sherry. Tell guests it is a New Orleans classic they should try at least once. For a pairing, a dry Sercial Madeira or an amontillado-style fortified wine echoes the sherry, and a lean white like Chablis cuts through the richness.

items.description: Bananas Foster is Brennan's most famous creation. The dessert menu prints that it was invented in 1951 at Brennan's, made with bananas, butter, brown sugar, cinnamon, rum and housemade vanilla ice cream, flambéed tableside, at $14.00 per person with a minimum of two people per order. The warm sauce is spooned over cold vanilla ice cream. It is also course five of the Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's tasting, paired there with Brennan's private blend Congregation coffee and chicory. Sell the show as much as the taste. For a glass, a tawny Port, Boal Madeira or Sauternes all echo the caramel.

items.description: Fried pickles are a Southern bar staple, born in the Mississippi Delta and Arkansas. The Bubbles at Brennan's page prints Fried Pickles as a medley of housemade pickles with chive cream, at $14.00, among the bar snacks. Rather than only dill pickle chips, the medley suggests several pickled vegetables from the kitchen, battered and fried until crisp. The chive cream is a cool, mild dip that balances the sharp, salty tang of the pickles. Expect crunchy, sour, salty bites, the kind that make you want another sip. Recommend them for guests who want something light and fun with drinks. For a pairing, nothing beats Champagne with fried, salty food: the bubbles and acidity scrub the palate clean. A crisp Grüner Veltliner or a Riviera from the Bubbles cocktail list also works well.

items.description: The Roost Burger is the bar's signature sandwich, named for the Roost Bar in the courtyard. The Bubbles at Brennan's page prints it as two beef short rib patties, bacon, cheese, pickles, onions, tomato jam and special sauce, at $17.00. Short rib is a richly marbled cut, so the patties are juicy and deeply beefy; using two thinner patties gives more browned, crusty surface. Bacon adds smoke and salt, the pickles and onions bring crunch and sharpness, and tomato jam is a sweet, tangy, cooked tomato spread that stands in for ketchup. The special sauce is the house's own; ask the kitchen what is in it before describing it. Expect a rich, savory, slightly sweet burger built for a bar. For a drink, a Zinfandel like Ridge Lytton Springs or a Napa Cabernet is a classic match, and a Classic Sazerac is a strong New Orleans option.

items.description: A basket of fries is the simplest snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list, which prints French Fries with Pink Sauce at $8.00 among the bar snacks. Pink sauce is a common New Orleans dip, a cousin of Thousand Island and the classic Louisiana rémoulade: usually mayonnaise blended with ketchup or chili sauce, a little horseradish, lemon and seasoning, which gives it its pink color and a tangy, creamy, gently spicy flavor. The house recipe is not in the snippet, so ask the kitchen before naming ingredients. Expect hot, crisp, salty fries and a cool, tangy dip. Recommend it as an easy add-on for the table or the bar, especially with a bottle of Champagne during Bubbles at Brennan's: fried potatoes and sparkling wine are one of the great high-low pairings. A Pierre Sparr Crémant rosé by the glass is a cheerful alternative.

items.description: The Bubbles at Brennan's page prints the Cheese Board at $24.00 among the bar snacks: a selection of three cheeses, seasonal chutney, Brennan's honey, and fruit and nut bread. The cheeses themselves rotate, so learn tonight's three at lineup and how each is made: the milk (cow, goat or sheep), the texture (soft, semi-firm, hard) and where it comes from. Chutney is a sweet and tangy fruit preserve cooked with vinegar and spices, a good partner for aged and salty cheeses. The honey is printed as Brennan's honey, so ask about its source before telling a guest anything more. Fruit and nut bread gives a dense, slightly sweet base. Describe it as a relaxed, shareable board for the courtyard. For wine, cheese is where the cellar shines: Champagne for soft cheeses, a tawny Port or Madeira for aged and blue cheeses, a Sauternes for blue, and a red Burgundy or Rhône for firm cheeses.
